dryptosaurus:eswiki:8.title: Dryptosaurus aquilunguis (Impacto en la cultura popular)

facts.statement: Fossils of Dryptosaurus were discovered by fertilizer miners in New Jersey within the New Egypt Formation.
facts.quote: These fossils were unearthed by fertilizer miners in New Jersey in rock layers of the New Egypt Formation.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus lived during the late Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, approximately 67 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: This formation dates to the late Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous, around 67 to 66 million years ago.

facts.statement: Unlike other tyrannosaurs, Dryptosaurus had large forelimbs with big claws and slender hindlimbs.
facts.quote: Unlike other tyrannosaurs like Tyrannosaurus and Tarbosaurus, Dryptosaurus possessed large forelimbs ending in large claws and lithe hindlimbs.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus is estimated to have been 7.5 meters long and weighed between 756 and 1500 kilograms.
facts.quote: Size estimates place it at 7.5 m in length and 756 - 1500 kg in mass.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus possessed sharp, blade-like, laterally compressed teeth that differed from those of larger tyrannosaurs.
facts.quote: The genus had ziphodont (sharp, blade-like, laterally compressed) dentition, dissimilar to that of larger tyrannosaurs.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus belongs to the clade Eutyrannosauria, which includes Tyrannosauridae and genera like Nanotyrannus but excludes more basal tyrannosaurs like Dilong.
facts.quote: Dryptosaurus is a member of Eutyrannosauria, the clade including Tyrannosauridae and tyrannosaurs like Nanotyrannus and Bistahieversor but excluding more basal tyrannosaurs like Dilong.

facts.statement: Some studies classify Dryptosaurus in its own family, Dryptosauridae, or within Nanotyrannidae.
facts.quote: However, some studies have also put it in its own family, Dryptosauridae, or in Nanotyrannidae.

facts.statement: In the summer of 1866, workers from the West Jersey Marl Company found a theropod skeleton near Barnsboro, New Jersey, in the New Egypt Formation.
facts.quote: During the summer of 1866, workers from the West Jersey Marl Company uncovered an associated theropod skeleton in sediments coming from the New Egypt Formation in a quarry near Barnsboro, New Jersey.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope named the dinosaur Laelaps aquilunguis on August 21, 1866, after presenting its description to the American Philosophical Society.
facts.quote: On 21 August 1866, Cope presented his description of ANSP 9995 to the American Philosophical Society at what is now the Academy of Natural Sciences, naming it a new genus and species of dinosaur, Laelaps aquilunguis.

facts.statement: Othniel Marsh renamed the genus Dryptosaurus in 1877 because the original name Laelaps was already used for a mite.
facts.quote: In 1877, Marsh pointed out that Cope's genus name Laelaps was preoccupied by a genus of mite, leading to Marsh to erect the genus name Dryptosaurus.

facts.statement: The type specimen, cataloged as ANSP 9995, includes skull fragments, teeth, tail vertebrae, arm bones, an incomplete hand, a partial pelvis, and a nearly complete left hindlimb.
facts.quote: The skeleton was then deposited at the Academy of Natural Sciences in Philadelphia under the catalogue number ANSP 9995 and includes; skull and dentary fragments, teeth, caudal vertebrae, humeri, an incomplete manus, a partial pelvis, and nearly complete left hindlimb.

facts.statement: Sacral vertebrae originally assigned to Dryptosaurus are now thought to belong to the turtle Pneumatoarthrus.
facts.quote: Several sacral vertebrae Cope assigned to Dryptosaurus are now believed to belong to the protostegid turtle Pneumatoarthrus.

facts.statement: Some bones of the type specimen show evidence of molding, possibly done by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins for a failed museum project in Central Park.
facts.quote: Some of the bones have evidence of molding, which was possibly done by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins during his failed project to erect a Paleozoic Museum in Central Park, New York.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus is one of the few Cretaceous dinosaurs known from the Eastern United States.
facts.quote: Dryptosaurus is one of few Cretaceous dinosaurs known from the Eastern United States.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus fossils come from the marine New Egypt Formation, where dinosaur carcasses floated out to sea and were fossilized.
facts.quote: Fossils of Dryptosaurus are known from the marine New Egypt Formation where dinosaur bodies floated out to sea and became fossilized.

facts.statement: The only known species of Dryptosaurus is D. aquilunguis.
facts.quote: species: aquilunguis

facts.statement: The species D. aquilunguis was originally described by Cope in 1866 under the name Laelaps.
facts.quote: authority: (Cope, 1866 [originally Laelaps])

facts.statement: The species Laelaps trihedrodon was discovered by schoolteacher Oramel W. Lucas between 1877 and 1878 in the Late Jurassic Morrison Formation of Garden Park, Colorado.
facts.quote: Laelaps trihedrodon was first discovered by Oramel W. Lucas, a schoolteacher from Garden Park, Colorado, who collected an incomplete dentary with teeth from 1877 to 1878 in strata of the Late Jurassic-aged Morrison Formation in Garden Park.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope described the material as the new species Laelaps trihedrodon in 1877.
facts.quote: Cope described this material as belonging to a new species of Laelaps, Laelaps trihedrodon, "three-hedged tooth", in 1877.

facts.statement: Joseph Leidy described two theropod tibia found in the Maastrichtian-aged Navesink Formation of New Jersey as the new species Coelosaurus antiquus in 1865.
facts.quote: In 1865, Joseph Leidy described two theropod tibia that had been found in the Maastrichtian-aged Navesink Formation of New Jersey as belonging to a new genus and species of dinosaur, Coelosaurus antiquus.

facts.statement: In 1868, Cope reclassified the specimen originally named Coelosaurus antiquus as the species Laelaps macropus.
facts.quote: However, in 1868 Cope described this specimen (AMNH 2550-2553) as belonging to its own species of Laelaps (Dryptosaurus) which he named L. macropus.

facts.statement: Cope named Laelaps falculus in 1876 based on ten isolated teeth found by Jno. C. Issac in the Campanian-aged Judith River Formation of Montana.
facts.quote: In 1876, Cope named Laelaps falculus on the basis of ten isolated teeth that had been found by Jno. C. Issac from the "Fort Union Beds" (now considered the Judith River Formation) of Montana dating to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: Cope named Laelaps incrassatus in 1876 based on two isolated maxillary teeth found by Jno. C. Issac in the Campanian-aged Judith River Formation of Montana.
facts.quote: In 1876, Cope named Laelaps incrassatus on the basis of two isolated maxillary teeth that had been found by Jno. C. Issac from the "Fort Union Beds" (now considered the Judith River Formation) of Montana dating to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: Cope named Laelaps explanatus in 1876 based on several teeth found in the Campanian-aged Judith River Formation of Montana.
facts.quote: In 1876, Cope named Laelaps explanatus on the basis of several teeth that had been found in rocks of the "Fort Union Beds" (now considered the Judith River Formation) of Montana dating to the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: Cope described Laelaps hazenianus in 1876 based on seven teeth from the Late Campanian Judith River Group of Montana.
facts.quote: Laelaps hazenianus was described by Cope in 1876 on the basis of seven teeth from the Judith River Group of Montana dating to the Late Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: Donald Baird and John R. Horner described numerous fossils from the Campanian-aged Tar Heel/Coachman Formation in North Carolina in 1979.
facts.quote: In 1979, Donald Baird and John R. Horner described a multitude of fossils from the Campanian-aged Tar Heel/Coachman Formation in North Carolina, United States.

facts.statement: In February 2018, Brownstein tentatively classified partial teeth and femur fragments from the 1979 specimens as Dryptosaurus aquilunguis.
facts.quote: In February 2018, based on specimens described by Baird and Horner (1979), Brownstein tentatively classified the partial teeth (USNM 7199 and ANSP 15332) as D. sp. and the partial femur fragments (ANSP 15330 and USNM 7189, the latter of which was in part a syntype of Hypsibema) as D. aquilunguis.

facts.statement: In 2001, Chure argued that the holotype specimen AMNH 5780 probably belongs to Allosaurus rather than Laelaps trihedrodon.
facts.quote: In 2001, Chure argued that AMNH 5780 probably belongs to Allosaurus.

facts.statement: It is debated whether Laelaps falculus is a valid species, with some suggesting it is a nomen dubium based on juvenile tyrannosaur teeth.
facts.quote: However, L. falculus is a nomen dubium and likely is based on juvenile tyrannosaur teeth.

facts.statement: Most putative Dryptosaurus specimens from the Tar Heel/Coachman Formation are now considered indeterminate Eutyrannosauria separate from Dryptosaurus, with some suggesting they belong to Appalachiosaurus.
facts.quote: It was suggested that the indeterminate specimens from Marshalltown Formation might belong to Appalachiosaurus instead, and most of the putative specimens (ANSP 15330, ANSP 15332 and USNM 7199) from the Tar Heel/Coachman Formation were subsequently referred to as indeterminate Eutyrannosauria separate from Dryptosaurus, with only USNM 7189 tentatively classified as D. sp.

facts.statement: The combination Megalosaurus saharicus proposed by Depéret and Savornin in 1927 is now classified in the genus Carcharodontosaurus.
facts.quote: Megalosaurus (Dryptosaurus) saharicus was an alternative combination for Megalosaurus saharicus proposed by Charles Depéret and Justin Savornin in 1927, however it is now classified in its own genus, Carcharodontosaurus.

facts.statement: The combination Erectopus superbus proposed by Depéret and Savornin in 1927 is now classified in the genus Erectopus.
facts.quote: Erectopus (Dryptosaurus) superbus was an alternative combination for Megalosaurus superbus proposed by Depéret and Savornin in 1927, however it is now classified in its own genus, Erectopus.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus is estimated to have reached a length of 7.5 meters and a weight between 756 and 1500 kilograms based on partial remains of a single individual.
facts.quote: Dryptosaurus is estimated to have been 7.5 m long and 756 - 1500 kg, although this is based on partial remains of one individual.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus possessed relatively long arms compared to more derived tyrannosaurs like Tyrannosaurus, similar to its relative Eotyrannus.
facts.quote: Like its relative Eotyrannus, Dryptosaurus seems to have had relatively long arms when compared with more derived tyrannosaurs, such as Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: Each finger of Dryptosaurus was tipped with a talon-like claw measuring eight inches in length.
facts.quote: Each of its fingers were tipped with an eight-inch long, talon-like claw.

facts.statement: The longest recovered manual claw (ungual phalanx) of Dryptosaurus measured 176 millimeters in length.
facts.quote: The longest manual ungual phalanx recovered measured 176 mm in length.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus had transversely narrow, recurved teeth with serrations consisting of 17 to 18 denticles per centimeter.
facts.quote: The disarticulated teeth recovered are transversely narrow, serrated (17–18 denticles/cm), and recurved.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Dryptosaurus likely used both its arms and jaws as weapons for hunting, capturing, and processing prey.
facts.quote: Dryptosaurus may have used both its arms and its jaws as weapons when hunting, capturing, and processing its prey.

facts.statement: The type specimen of Dryptosaurus is a fragmentary skeleton of a single adult individual cataloged as ANSP 9995.
facts.quote: The type specimen is a fragmentary skeleton belonging to a single adult individual, ANSP 9995.

facts.statement: Othniel Charles Marsh established the family Dryptosauridae in 1890 to classify large theropod dinosaurs including Dryptosaurus.
facts.quote: Marsh (1890) dubbed a new family, Dryptosauridae, for some large theropod dinosaurs.

facts.statement: Charles W. Gilmore was the first to observe anatomical links between Dryptosaurus and Late Cretaceous tyrannosaurids such as Albertosaurus and Tyrannosaurus.
facts.quote: Charles W. Gilmore was the first to observe that certain anatomical features may link Dryptosaurus with coeval Late Cretaceous tyrannosaurids, Albertosaurus, and Tyrannosaurus.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analysis by Brusatte et al. (2013) confirmed Dryptosaurus as an intermediate tyrannosauroid, more derived than basal taxa like Guanlong and Dilong but more primitive than derived Tyrannosauridae members.
facts.quote: This discovery made it clear that Dryptosaurus was also a basal tyrannosauroid, an idea supported by a detailed phylogenetic analysis from Brusatte et al. (2013) which confirmed the tyrannosauroid affinities of Dryptosaurus and assigned it as an "intermediate" tyrannosauroid that is more derived than basal taxa, such as Guanlong and Dilong, but more primitive than members of the more derived Tyrannosauridae.

facts.statement: While earlier beliefs suggested Dryptosaurus had three fingers, Brusatte et al. (2011) noted the phalange shape suggests it may have had only two functional digits.
facts.quote: Brusatte et al. (2011), however, observed an overall similarity in the shape of the available phalanges of Dryptosaurus with those of derived tyrannosaurids and noted that Dryptosaurus may have had only two functional digits.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus lived in eastern North America during the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: Dryptosaurus was the only large named tyrannosaur known in eastern North America until the description of the basal tyrannosauroid Appalachiosaurus in 2005.

facts.statement: The genus Dryptosaurus was named by Othniel Charles Marsh in 1877.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Marsh, 1877

facts.statement: The species Dryptosaurus aquilunguis was named by Edward Drinker Cope in 1866.
facts.quote: species_authority: Cope, 1866

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus aquilunguis was originally described as Laelaps aquilunguis and later as Megalosaurus aquilunguis before being reclassified.
facts.quote: synonyms: Laelaps aquilunguis Cope, 1866 (preocupado) Megalosaurus aquilunguis (Cope, 1866)

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus lived in North America during the Late Cretaceous, approximately 67 million years ago in the Maastrichtian stage.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 67 millones de años, en el Maastrichtiense, en lo que hoy es Norteamérica

facts.statement: Fossils of Dryptosaurus were discovered while mining glauconitic marl for fertilizer at the West Jersey Marl Company Pit.
facts.quote: Mining of the glauconitic marls in the West Jersey Marl Company Pit for fertilizers led to the discovery of fossils like those of Dryptosaurus.

facts.statement: The Dryptosaurus holotype fossilized after the individual floated out to sea and sank to the sea floor.
facts.quote: The Dryptosaurus holotype was an individual that floated out to sea, sunk to the sea floor, and became fossilized.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus likely preyed on hadrosaurids, ornithomimosaurs, and ankylosaurs.
facts.quote: Dryptosaurus and the Merchantville taxon likely preyed on hadrosaurids, ornithomimosaurs, and ankylosaurs, which are all represented by fragmentary remains.

facts.statement: The size of Dryptosaurus is comparable to that of Laramidian tyrannosauroids.
facts.quote: the size of Dryptosaurus is in line with those of Laramidian tyrannosauroids

facts.statement: A famous painting by Charles R. Knight made Dryptosaurus one of the most famous dinosaurs of its time despite its poor fossil record.
facts.quote: una famosa pintura del género por Charles R. Knight lo convirtió en uno de los dinosaurios más conocidos de su tiempo, a pesar de su pobre registro fósil

facts.statement: It is debated whether Dryptosauridae is a valid clade, as many subsequent papers recover Dryptosaurus as a basal eutyrannosaur outside this family.
facts.quote: However, many subsequent papers have not included Dryptosauridae, instead recovering Dryptosaurus it as a basal eutyrannosaur.

facts.statement: Researchers note that further testing and more data are required to support specific phylogenetic analyses regarding Dryptosaurus relationships.
facts.quote: The authors noted that further testing and more data would be required to support the results of one analysis over the other.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus is estimated to have reached 7.5 meters in length and weighed 1.5 tonnes, though this is based on partial remains of a single individual.
facts.quote: Se estima que Dryptosaurus llegó a medir 7,5 metros de largo y pesar 1,5 toneladas, aunque esto se basa en restos parciales de un individuo.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus is believed to have had large hands with three fingers and claws nearly 20 centimeters long.
facts.quote: Sus manos, que también son relativamente grandes, se cree que tenían tres dedos con grandes garras de cerca de 20 centímetros.

facts.statement: Researchers Brusatte and colleagues in 2011 suggested that Dryptosaurus may have had only two functional digits despite having three finger bones, similar to derived tyrannosaurids.
facts.quote: Brusatte y colegas en 2011, sin embargo, observaron una similitud general en la forma de las falanges disponibles de Dryptosaurus con las de los tiranosáuridos derivados y señalaron que Dryptosaurus puede haber tenido solo dos dígitos funcionales.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus likely used both its arms and jaws as weapons to hunt, capture, and tear apart prey.
facts.quote: Dryptosaurus puede haber usado tanto sus brazos como sus mandíbulas como armas al cazar, capturar y desgarrar las presas.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen ANSP 9995 is a fragmentary adult skeleton containing parts of the skull, 11 distal-caudal vertebrae, left and right humeri, three left hand phalanges, pubic bones, a right ischium, left femur, left tibia, left fibula, left astragalus, and a fragment of the left metatarsal III.
facts.quote: El espécimen tipo es un esqueleto fragmentario que pertenece a un solo individuo adulto, ANSP 9995 que consiste en un maxilar derecho fragmentario, un dentario derecho fragmentario, un surangular derecho fragmentario, dientes laterales, 11 vértebras caudales medio-distales, los húmero izquierdo y derecho, tres falanges manuales de la mano izquierda, I-1, II-2 y ungual, los ejes de los huesos púbicos izquierdo y derecho , un isquion derecho fragmentario , el fémur izquierdo , la tibia izquierda , el peroné izquierdo , el astrágalo izquierdo , y un fragmento de la mitad del metatarso III.

facts.statement: The longest recovered manual ungual phalanx of Dryptosaurus measured 176 millimeters in length.
facts.quote: La falange ungual manual más larga recuperada midió 176 milímetros de longitud.

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus likely had an arctometatarsalian foot, an advanced trait shared with derived tyrannosaurids like Albertosaurus and Tyrannosaurus where the third metatarsal is pinched between the second and fourth.
facts.quote: La morfología de la parte proximal del metatarsiano IV sugiere que Dryptosaurus tenía un pie arctometatarsaliano, una característica avanzada compartida por tiranosáuridos derivados como Albertosaurus y Tyrannosaurus, en la que el tercer metatarsiano se "pellizca" entre el segundo y cuarto.

facts.statement: An incomplete skeleton of Dryptosaurus, specimen ANSP 9995, was found in New Jersey in 1866 by workers in a quarry.
facts.quote: En 1866, un incompleto esqueleto, ANSP 9995, fue encontrado en Nueva Jersey por trabajadores en una cantera.

facts.statement: Because the name "Laelaps" was already used for a mite, rival paleontologist Othniel Charles Marsh renamed the species Dryptosaurus aquilunguis in 1877.
facts.quote: Subsecuentemente, fue descubierto que el nombre "Laelaps" ya había sido dado también a un ácaro, y el rival de E. D. Cope, Othniel Charles Marsh lo renombró como Dryptosaurus aquilunguis en 1877.

facts.statement: The genus name Dryptosaurus means "tear lizard" and is derived from the Greek words for "tear" and "lizard."
facts.quote: El nombre del género Dryptosaurus, significa "lagarto lágrima", y se deriva de las palabras griegas dryptō , δρύπτω, que significa "lágrima" y sauros, σαυρος, que significa "lagarto".

facts.statement: The specific name D. aquilunguis means "having claws like an eagle," referring to the three-fingered hand.
facts.quote: El nombre específico D. aquilunguis, se deriva del latín para "tener garras como las de un águila", una referencia a las garras en su mano de tres dedos.

facts.statement: The species Dryptosaurus trihedrodon was named by Cope in 1877, but most of the material is lost, and the remaining teeth are likely referable to Allosaurus.
facts.quote: Dryptosaurus (Laelaps) trihedrodon: nombrada por Cope en 1877. Aunque el espécimen incluye un dentario parcial, todo el material, exceptuando una colección de cinco coronas dentales parciales y dañadas, AMNH 5780, se ha perdido, aunque estas pueden no pertenecer al mismo animal.

facts.statement: The species Dryptosaurus incrassatus was assigned to Gorgosaurus libratus.
facts.quote: Dryptosaurus incrassatus: asignado a Gorgosaurus libratus

facts.statement: The species Dryptosaurus falculus was assigned to Gorgosaurus libratus.
facts.quote: Dryptosaurus falculus: asignado a Gorgosaurus libratus

facts.statement: The species Dryptosaurus hazenianus was assigned to Gorgosaurus libratus.
facts.quote: Dryptosaurus hazenianus: asignado a Gorgosaurus libratus

facts.statement: The species Dryptosaurus kenabekides was assigned to Gorgosaurus libratus.
facts.quote: Dryptosaurus kenabekides: asignado a Gorgosaurus libratus

facts.statement: The species Dryptosaurus explanatus was assigned to Paronychodon explanatus.
facts.quote: Dryptosaurus explanatus: asignado a Paronychodon explanatus

facts.statement: The species Dryptosaurus cristatus was assigned to Troodon ssp.
facts.quote: Dryptosaurus cristatus: asignado a Troodon ssp.

facts.statement: Edward Drinker Cope initially classified Dryptosaurus as a megalosaurid based on similarities with Megalosaurus.
facts.quote: Cope lo clasificó como un megalosáurido.

facts.statement: The parent group of the genus Dryptosaurus is Tyrannosauroidea.
facts.quote: Parent group: Tyrannosauroidea

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus is classified within the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: Dryptosaurus lived from the Albian to the Maastrichtian stages, approximately 113.2 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Albian to Maastrichtian (113.2 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: The type specimen of Dryptosaurus (ANSP 9995) was recovered from the West Jersey Marl Company Pit in the Hornerstown Formation, Barnsboro, Gloucester County, New Jersey.
facts.quote: El espécimen tipo de Dryptosaurus ANSP 9995 fue recuperado en West Jersey Marl Company Pit, en lo que se conoce como la Formación Hornerstown en Barnsboro, en el condado de Gloucester, Nueva Jersey.

facts.statement: The type specimen was found in sediments deposited during the Maastrichtian stage of the Cretaceous, approximately 67 million years ago.
facts.quote: El espécimen fue recogido por trabajadores de la cantera de margas y areniscas que se depositaron durante el Maastrichtiano, última etapa del periodo Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 67 millones de años.

facts.statement: Nodosaurids were present in the environment but likely hunted less frequently by Dryptosaurus due to their heavy armor.
facts.quote: Aparte de los hadrosáuridos, los nodosáuridos estaban también presentes aunque debían haber sido cazados en menor medida por su fuerte armadura.

facts.statement: Current efforts led by Gary Vecchiarelli aim to mount the Dryptosaurus skeleton permanently at the New Jersey State Museum in Trenton.
facts.quote: Los esfuerzos actuales están en curso bajo la dirección de Gary Vecchiarelli del Proyecto Dryptosaurus, para conseguir un montaje del esqueleto estableciéndolo en una ubicación más permanente alojada en el Museo Estatal de Nueva Jersey en Trenton.

rejected.quote: In 1892, Cope assigned two incomplete tyrannosaur skulls from rocks of the Horseshoe Canyon Formation in Alberta, Canada to L. incrassatus on the basis of their similar tooth anatomy.

rejected.quote: A 2018 paper tentatively assigned two isolated teeth from the Ellisdale Site in Monmouth County, New Jersey, which contains strata of the Maastrichthian-aged Marshalltown Formation, to Dryptosaurus.

rejected.quote: However that same year Chase Brownstein argued that "Teihivenator macropus" is actually a chimera and a nomen dubium.
